name: Proper scoring rules and CORP reliability diagrams. Core: Gneiting & Raftery (2007), 'Strictly Proper Scoring Rules, Prediction, and Estimation' (JASA 102(477):359-378), and Dimitriadis, Gneiting & Jordan (2021), 'Stable reliability diagrams for probabilistic classifiers' (PNAS 118(8):e2016191118; arXiv preprint title 'Evaluating probabilistic classifiers: Reliability diagrams and score decompositions revisited'). Companions: Dimitriadis, Gneiting, Jordan & Vogel (2024), 'Evaluating probabilistic classifiers: The triptych' (IJF 40(3):1101-1122), and Dimitriadis, Duembgen, Henzi, Puke & Ziegel (2023), 'Honest calibration assessment for binary outcome predictions' (Biometrika 110(3):663-680)
type: method family (forecast-evaluation theory: proper scoring rules, skill scores, PAV/isotonic reliability diagrams, the CORP score decomposition MCB - DSC + UNC)
url: Gneiting & Raftery 2007: https://doi.org/10.1198/016214506000001437 (author PDF: https://sites.stat.washington.edu/raftery/Research/PDF/Gneiting2007jasa.pdf) ; CORP: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2016191118 (open access: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7923594/ ; preprint: https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.03033) ; Triptych: https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.10803 (replication code: https://github.com/TimoDimi/replication_triptych) ; Honest calibration bands: https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.04065 (https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/asac068) ; R package: https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=reliabilitydiag ; Python implementation with isotonic reliability diagrams and score decomposition: https://lorentzenchr.github.io/model-diagnostics/
year: 2007 (Gneiting & Raftery); 2021 (CORP, PNAS, published 17 Feb 2021; arXiv v1 7 Aug 2020); 2023 (honest calibration bands, Biometrika); 2024 (triptych, IJF). R package reliabilitydiag 0.2.1, last published 2022-06-29.
authors: Tilmann Gneiting, Adrian E. Raftery (2007). Timo Dimitriadis, Tilmann Gneiting, Alexander I. Jordan (CORP, 2021; HITS and KIT). Plus Peter Vogel (triptych, 2024). Timo Dimitriadis, Lutz Duembgen, Alexander Henzi, Marius Puke, Johanna Ziegel (honest bands, 2023). reliabilitydiag is maintained by Alexander I. Jordan.
popularity: Semantic Scholar citations (retrieved 2026-10-17): Gneiting & Raftery 2007 = 7,406; CORP (PNAS) = 111; triptych = 22. Gneiting & Raftery is one of the most cited papers in forecast evaluation. CORP is the current reference method for reliability diagrams in the probabilistic-forecasting literature (statistics, meteorology, economics).
peer_review_status: peer-reviewed (JASA; PNAS; IJF; Biometrika). CORP and the triptych also have arXiv preprints.
target_type: Not a forecasting application. The methods are generic for binary-event probability forecasts and suit our onset target directly: y in {0,1}, forecast p in [0,1]. Proper scoring rules and CORP diagrams do not stop a state target from inflating scores. They score whatever label they are given, so the onset vs state choice and the at-risk mask (CLAUDE.md Target) must be fixed before scoring. A state target would have a high-persistence, easy-to-discriminate structure, and CORP would report it as high DSC rather than flag it.
target_definition: Generic binary event Y = 1 with forecast probability p. The Brier (quadratic) score is S(p, y) = (p - y)^2, negatively oriented. The log score is -log p if y = 1 and -log(1 - p) if y = 0. In the CORP paper's worked example the event is 'precipitation occurs' at Niamey, Niger, issued 24 h ahead daily, July-September 2016, n = 92. For our project the event is 'a new alert starts in (t, t+H]', H = 1 h, per oblast-hour.
spatial_unit: Not applicable (method papers). The CORP example is a single station (Niamey). The methods apply to any pooled or per-unit set of forecast-observation pairs, so for us: pooled, per group (Kyiv City / frontline / rear), and per oblast.
at_risk_masking: Not applicable in the papers. The scoring theory assumes a fixed set of evaluation cases, and all comparisons are valid only on the IDENTICAL set of rows. For us, the model and every baseline must be scored on exactly the same unmasked rows: the same at-risk mask, the same gap mask, and the same label-maturity rule. Then mean Brier, BSS and the CORP terms are directly comparable.
data_sources: Gneiting & Raftery 2007: illustrative examples (e.g. probabilistic weather and quantile forecasts) [uncertain: the exact datasets were not re-checked]. CORP 2021: daily 24-h probability-of-precipitation forecasts at Niamey, July-September 2016 (n = 92), from Vogel et al. (2021). Four forecasts: ENS (52-member ECMWF ensemble), EPC (an extended probabilistic climatology reference), EMOS (postprocessed ENS) and Logistic (a statistical model). The supplement has further meteorological, geophysical, social-science and economic datasets. Triptych 2024: astrophysics (solar flares [uncertain]), economics and social-science examples.
preprocessing: Not applicable. Method note: CORP needs no binning choice. The PAV algorithm pools forecast values into flat segments automatically, and identical forecast values (ties) stay in the same segment. That matters for our tie-heavy baselines: climatology takes one of only 168 hour x weekday values per oblast, raw persistence is 0/1, and the shrunken recent rate is discrete.
known_label_artefacts: Not applicable to air alerts. The relevant artefact is in the EVALUATION method: binning-and-counting instability. In the CORP paper, the EMOS reliability diagram for Niamey looks 'drastically distinct' with 9, 10 or 11 equal-width bins, one version showing a spurious spike in a sparsely populated bin. Equal-population bins do not fully fix this, because identical forecast values often fall on bin edges. The instability carries over to the binned Brier reliability component and to the Hosmer-Lemeshow statistic. Our current reliability_bins() in src/evaluate.py uses 10 fixed-width bins on [0,1]. With hourly onset base rates of a few percent, most rows fall in the [0, 0.1) bin, so the D-006 plot is controlled by bin choice. This is the artefact CORP removes.
model_family: Evaluation methodology, not a model. (1) Proper scoring rules (Gneiting & Raftery 2007): a score is proper if the true distribution minimises the expected score, and strictly proper if that minimum is unique. Both the Brier and log scores are strictly proper for binary events. The log score is the only proper local score (it depends only on the probability given to the realised outcome), and it is unbounded when p = 0 or 1. Skill scores of the form SS = 1 - S_forecast / S_reference are generally NOT proper when applied case by case, even if S is (the paper credits Murphy 1973) [uncertain: exact section not re-checked]. Mean scores over a fixed test set are the recommended way to compare forecasters, under the 'maximise sharpness subject to calibration' paradigm (Gneiting, Balabdaoui & Raftery 2007). (2) CORP (2021): Consistent, Optimally binned, Reproducible reliability diagrams via the PAV algorithm. Isotonic regression of y on p gives recalibrated probabilities p_hat = PAV(p). The reliability diagram is the step function p -> p_hat. The mean score decomposes exactly as S_bar = MCB - DSC + UNC, where MCB = S_bar(p) - S_bar(p_hat) >= 0, DSC = S_bar(y_bar) - S_bar(p_hat) >= 0, and UNC = S_bar(y_bar) (for Brier, y_bar(1 - y_bar)). The decomposition holds for any proper scoring rule. For the Brier score, MCB and DSC coincide with Murphy's REL and RES once the binning is the PAV one.
features: Not applicable (no forecasting features). Method components that matter for us: (a) PAV / isotonic regression: scikit-learn IsotonicRegression(increasing=True, out_of_bounds='clip'), or scipy.optimize.isotonic_regression, which needs SciPy >= 1.12 [uncertain]. (b) Uncertainty: consistency bands (centred on the diagonal; resample y* ~ Bernoulli(p) under the null of calibration, recompute PAV, take pointwise quantiles) and confidence bands (resample around the CORP estimate using the PAV-calibrated probabilities). (c) Asymptotics: for discrete forecasts the error scaled by n^(1/2) is a normal mixture. For continuous forecasts it is scaled by n^(1/3) with Chernoff's distribution. The software uses resampling for small n and switches to the discrete asymptotics when n >= 8k^2, where k = the number of distinct forecast values. (d) A generalised in-sample R* = (DSC - MCB) / UNC, which is the skill score against the in-sample marginal-frequency reference.
external_feature_timing: Not applicable. One timing caveat applies to how we use CORP. The UNC reference y_bar is the marginal event frequency OF THE EVALUATION SET, and the PAV recalibration is fitted in-sample on the evaluation set. Both are diagnostics computed after the fact. They are not causal forecasts and must never be reported as a baseline or applied as a recalibration (CLAUDE.md forbids statistics computed over the test period). Recalibration, if used, is fitted on validation only (D-021).
ablation_design: Not applicable. The triptych paper recommends comparing competitors on the same cases with an MCB-DSC scatter plot. Isolines of equal mean score are diagonal lines DSC - MCB = constant, so one plot shows whether a model wins through better ranking (DSC) or better calibration (MCB). The same plot works for feature ablations evaluated on identical rows.
split_scheme: Not applicable. All the CORP inference (bands and asymptotics) assumes independent, or at least exchangeable, forecast cases. The authors say this 'may or may not be warranted' and call for future work on serially dependent data. Our test rows are strongly dependent in time (attack waves) and across oblasts (mass attacks), so the default iid resampling bands will be too narrow.
metrics: Brier score, log score, Brier skill score, CORP MCB / DSC / UNC (with the corresponding Murphy REL / RES / UNC), the in-sample R*, and reliability diagrams with consistency or confidence bands. The triptych adds ROC curves (discrimination) and Murphy curves. The area under the Murphy curve equals the mean Brier score (up to scaling), and the curve shows the economic value across cost-loss ratios. The CORP paper names the MCB measure as a candidate for a calibration test. The R package ships miscalibration_test(). Dimitriadis et al. 2023 give isotonicity-based calibration bands with finite-sample coverage guarantees, which also support a test of perfect calibration.
unit_of_metric: Pooled over the evaluation set. The decomposition must be recomputed (a new PAV fit) for every subset, because MCB and DSC are not additive across groups: per-group MCBs do not sum to the pooled MCB.
baseline_strength: CORP Table 2 (Niamey, Brier, UNC = 0.244 for all): ENS mean score 0.266 (MCB 0.066, DSC 0.044), EPC 0.234 (0.022, 0.032), EMOS 0.232 (0.018, 0.030), Logistic 0.206 (0.017, 0.056). The raw ensemble does WORSE than the climatological uncertainty 0.244 because its miscalibration (0.066) exceeds its discrimination (0.044). EMOS and Logistic are equally well calibrated, and Logistic wins on discrimination. This shows how the decomposition explains a skill difference against a reference.
calibration: Main contribution. A CORP reliability diagram plots the PAV-recalibrated probability against the forecast probability, with no tuning parameters. It is consistent (it converges to the true conditional event probability), optimally binned (at rate n^(-2/3) in simulation it has lower MSE than 5, 10 or 50 fixed bins or quantile bins), and reproducible (the same data always give the same diagram). Recommended display: the CORP step curve, a 90% consistency band around the diagonal, a histogram or rug of the forecast values, and the MCB, DSC, UNC numbers in the panel. In simulations with 1,000 replicates, 90% bands had accurate or slightly conservative coverage under independence. The PAV fit is also the in-sample isotonic recalibration map. It may be used as a recalibrator only when it is fitted on a separate (validation) slice.
calibration_under_drift: Not addressed directly. Mean predicted vs observed (calibration-in-the-large) is part of MCB, not a separate term in CORP. Later work by Gneiting and co-authors splits MCB into unconditional and conditional parts (UMCB + CMCB) [uncertain: from memory, Gneiting et al. 2023, Annual Review of Statistics, 'Model diagnostics and forecast evaluation for quantiles'; not re-checked here]. For D-015 (c) the CORP curve shows the direction of drift: the curve lying entirely below the diagonal means systematic over-prediction after the reform, while a crossing curve means a changed slope (discrimination preserved, scale wrong).
uncertainty_of_gain: Gneiting & Raftery 2007 recommend comparing mean scores on the same cases. Formal tests of equal predictive performance (Diebold-Mariano) are in the wider literature, not in CORP. CORP gives bands for the reliability curve, not for score differences. Its bands assume independence, so for dependent data they understate uncertainty. This is the authors' own caveat, not an empirical finding about alert data.
regime_coverage: Not applicable (no alert data). Note that the Niamey example covers a single monsoon season (Jul-Sep 2016), and the methods say nothing about non-stationarity.
leakage_handling: Not applicable as a forecasting pipeline. The leakage risks in using these tools are: (1) Fitting the PAV recalibration map on the test set and reporting the recalibrated Brier as model performance. In-sample PAV is optimistic: S_bar(p_hat) is the best any monotone recalibration could reach on those rows, and DSC is mildly over-estimated in small samples. Report MCB/DSC as diagnostics only. (2) Using the evaluation-set marginal rate y_bar as a 'climatology' baseline, which uses future labels. Our climatology baseline must stay the train-fitted hour x weekday rate (CLAUDE.md Baselines). (3) Choosing bin counts or plotting options after looking at test results, which CORP removes because it has no free parameters. That also supports the 'score the final test once' rule.
test_window_hygiene: Not applicable. Because CORP is parameter-free, the D-006 reliability plot can be specified fully in the M4 plan BEFORE the final test is scored. No bin count or band level is chosen after seeing test numbers. Fix the band level (90%) and the resampling scheme (block bootstrap, see takeaways) in advance.
headline_results: (1) Gneiting & Raftery 2007: a unified theory of proper scoring rules (characterised through convex functions, with Savage/Schervish representations for binary events). Brier and log scores are strictly proper. Skill scores are generally improper on a per-case basis [uncertain: section number not re-checked]. Proper scores reward 'sharpness subject to calibration'. (2) CORP 2021: binned reliability diagrams are unstable. On Niamey EMOS, 9, 10 and 11 bins give very different pictures. The PAV-based diagram is stable, consistent and optimally binned. The exact decomposition S = MCB - DSC + UNC with MCB, DSC >= 0 holds for any proper score. Niamey Brier results: Logistic 0.206 (MCB 0.017, DSC 0.056) beats EMOS 0.232 (0.018, 0.030), EPC 0.234 (0.022, 0.032) and raw ENS 0.266 (0.066, 0.044), against UNC = 0.244. (3) Triptych 2024: reliability (CORP), ROC and Murphy curves plus the MCB-DSC plot are a complete diagnostic set for binary probability forecasts. For calibrated forecasts, the ROC and Murphy curves have the same number of crossings. (4) Honest bands 2023: isotonicity-only confidence bands for the calibration curve, with finite-sample coverage, narrower than earlier methods.
code_available: Yes. R: reliabilitydiag 0.2.1 on CRAN (GPL-3), with reliabilitydiag(), summary() for the MCB/DSC/UNC decomposition, plot() and miscalibration_test(). Replication code: GitHub TimoDimi/replication_DGJ20 (CORP) and TimoDimi/replication_triptych. Python: model-diagnostics (MIT), with plot_reliability_diagram(..., n_bootstrap=, confidence_level=) built on isotonic regression and decompose(y_obs, y_pred, scoring_function=...) for miscalibration/discrimination/uncertainty. No new dependency is needed for this project: CORP for Brier is about 15 lines with sklearn.isotonic.IsotonicRegression, already available through the pinned scikit-learn==1.9.1. Adding model-diagnostics would need the human's approval (CLAUDE.md).
takeaways_for_project:
1) Upgrade the D-006 reliability plot from 10 fixed-width bins to a CORP (PAV) reliability diagram. Our base rate is a few percent per oblast-hour, so the current reliability_bins() puts nearly all rows in [0, 0.1) and its shape depends on the bin choice. That is the instability the CORP paper documents. PAV handles our tie-heavy baselines (0/1 persistence, 168-value climatology, discrete shrunken recent rate) correctly by keeping ties together. Use a log-scaled or zoomed x-axis (for example 0-0.3) plus a rug or histogram of forecast values. Report MCB, DSC and UNC in each panel.
2) Decompose the PRIMARY metric (D-021). On identical rows, UNC is shared, so S_ref - S_model = (DSC_model - DSC_ref) - (MCB_model - MCB_ref), and BSS_vs_recent = [(DSC_m - DSC_r) - (MCB_m - MCB_r)] / S_ref. The README can then say whether the model beats (or fails to beat) the rolling recent-rate through ranking (DSC) or through calibration (MCB). The diagnosis is concrete: a high-DSC but high-MCB model needs recalibration on validation (D-021), not new features. Add one MCB-DSC scatter plot (triptych style) for the model and all four baselines, with iso-score lines.
3) Compute BSS as a ratio of MEAN Brier scores on the same rows, 1 - mean(BS_model) / mean(BS_recent), per group, as metric_table() already does. Never average per-row or per-oblast skill ratios. Per-case skill scores are improper (Gneiting & Raftery, after Murphy 1973), and averaging per-oblast ratios gives quiet rear oblasts with tiny reference Brier the same weight as busy ones. Because the reference (rolling recent-rate) does not depend on the model, ranking by aggregate BSS equals ranking by mean Brier, so the primary metric stays a proper comparison.
4) Keep the Brier score as the proper headline score. If log loss is added, clip p to [eps, 1 - eps] and say so. PAV-recalibrated probabilities can be exactly 0 or 1, so the log-score version of the CORP decomposition can be infinite on small per-oblast subsets. ROC-AUC and PR-AUC are not proper scores (they ignore calibration), so they stay secondary, as CLAUDE.md already says.
5) Bands under dependence (D-013). CORP's default bands assume independent cases, but onsets cluster across oblasts in the same hour and in time. The default 'resample y* ~ Bernoulli(p) per row' consistency band treats a mass attack as 24 independent coin flips and will look too tight. Use a confidence band from a week-block (or day-block) bootstrap that resamples whole time blocks across all 24 units together, refitting PAV in each replicate. Six test weeks are few, so label the band 'indicative'. If an iid consistency band is shown as well, label it as such. [Interpretation: the authors only flag the independence assumption; they did not test it on clustered data.]
6) Use CORP on the API new-regime check (D-015 (c)) and per group (D-013): a CORP curve per group (Kyiv City, frontline, rear), and the pooled one in addition. A curve below the diagonal means the frozen model over-predicts after the reform. Report calibration-in-the-large (mean predicted - observed) next to MCB, because MCB mixes the level shift with shape errors. MCB/DSC are not additive across groups, so compute each group with its own PAV fit.
7) Never treat CORP's in-sample outputs as forecasts. The PAV-recalibrated test Brier and the test-set y_bar reference use test labels. They are diagnostics, not a model or a baseline (CLAUDE.md forbids test-period statistics). If isotonic recalibration is adopted, fit it on validation [2026-06-29, 2026-07-27) and apply it to the same frozen model (D-021). Note that isotonic calibration on ~4 weeks of rare positives is step-like and can overfit, so prefer a check over a fitted calibration unless validation MCB is clearly large.
8) Fix the CORP settings (band level 90%, block length = 1 week, bootstrap reps, x-axis range) in the M4 plan before scoring. CORP has no bin count to tune after seeing test results, which fits the 'score the final test ONCE' rule.
best_practices: ADOPT: (a) Strictly proper scores (Brier) as the headline and mean score over a fixed, identical row set for every forecaster. (b) CORP/PAV reliability diagrams instead of fixed or quantile bins, with forecast-value histograms and the MCB / DSC / UNC numbers printed. (c) Report the exact decomposition S = MCB - DSC + UNC, and explain skill gains against the reference as a DSC gain minus an MCB change. (d) An MCB-DSC plot (triptych) to compare all predictors in one figure. (e) Optionally, Murphy curves to show value across decision thresholds, e.g. for whom a 5% vs 20% alert-risk threshold matters. (f) Uncertainty bands by resampling that respects the dependence structure (time blocks across all units). (g) Fit any recalibration out of sample (validation only), and use in-sample PAV only for diagnosis. (h) Implement with sklearn IsotonicRegression, which is already pinned, rather than adding a dependency. AVOID: (1) Fixed-width bins at low base rates, where nearly everything falls in the first bin. (2) Choosing the bin count after seeing results. (3) Averaging per-case or per-oblast skill ratios; use the ratio of mean scores instead. (4) Treating the in-sample PAV-recalibrated score or the test y_bar as an achievable forecast or a baseline. (5) iid Bernoulli bands on clustered spatio-temporal events presented as definitive. (6) Using AUC or PR-AUC as the deciding metric, since they ignore calibration and are not proper scores. (7) Unclipped log loss on near-0/1 probabilities.
